title: New Breathlessness and Swollen Legs / Treat the Congestion, Time the Echo

blocks.text: New Breathlessness and Swollen Legs / Treat the Congestion, Time the Echo

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-45 · Consultation · PACES Consultation (Station 2) · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) · 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; a reminder may be given at 13 min · Guidelines: NICE NG106 Chronic heart failure in adults: diagnosis and management (published 12 September 2018; last updated 3 September 2025); NICE CG187 Acute heart failure: diagnosis and management (published 8 October 2014; last updated 17 November 2021) · Related AMaC: None identified

Dear Doctor, a 71-year-old retired dinner lady. Three weeks of breathlessness on walking, needing two pillows at night, and swollen ankles. Previous heart attack. Pulse 94, BP 138/84, saturation 95 per cent in air. Please assess and advise. She has consented to see you.
Please take a history, perform a relevant examination and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. New breathlessness, orthopnoea and leg swelling after a heart attack should be treated as heart failure until tests show another cause; the natriuretic peptide level sets how fast the echocardiogram is needed.

The Examiner Trap. She is stable and wants to go home. Candidates send her to the GP without a diuretic or a dated echo. Pass: treat the congestion, measure NT-proBNP, arrange specialist assessment and echo; do not use outpatient timescales to delay acute care, give a safety net. Fail: discharge without a plan.

rows: Heart, lung, kidney or clot? Get the story.
"Tell me about the breathlessness and swelling. Any chest pain, palpitations, cough or calf pain?"
Introduce, consent, ask about pain; orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, previous heart attack, drugs, smoking.
Is she congested, and is she stable?
"May I check your pulse, pressure, neck veins, chest and legs?"
Pulse, BP, JVP, heart sounds, crackles, effusions, oedema, liver, calves.
Treat now; test; time the echo.
"This looks like fluid retention that may be due to heart failure. A water tablet can relieve fluid retention; we need prompt assessment, blood tests and an ultrasound of the heart."
NT-proBNP, ECG, chest film, bloods; loop diuretic; echo by timescale; vaccines.
Share the plan; find her worry.
Explain tests and treatment; safety net; check understanding.
Makes her lie flat while breathless; no consent
Introduces, obtains consent, cleans hands, asks about pain, lets her sit up, covers her
Offers a chaperone, checks she is comfortable and thanks her
No orthopnoea, chest pain or drug history
Asks orthopnoea, nocturnal breathlessness, chest pain, previous heart attack, drugs and smoking
Also asks about palpitations, calf pain, anti-inflammatories, alcohol and weight change
Acknowledges worry; asks what concerns her
Finds the fear of ending like her husband, who died of heart failure, and answers honestly
Reports a normal JVP when it is raised
Pulse, BP, raised JVP, bibasal crackles, pitting oedema; no calf swelling
Adds heart sounds, effusion signs, liver and states negatives: no fever, no wheeze, no calf tenderness
Heart failure after a previous heart attack
Heart failure against pulmonary embolism, chronic lung disease, anaemia and kidney disease, with reasons
Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): discharges a congested patient with no assessment, diuretic or echo date
NT-proBNP; ECG; chest film; loop diuretic; stops ibuprofen; specialist assessment and echo within the chronic-pathway timescale if appropriate; earlier acute assessment when needed
Adds renal function before and after treatment, specialist referral, vaccines and a safety net
Benefits, risks and alternatives of home or admission; checks understanding
Covers what the echo will show, treatment steps after it, doing nothing and when to return

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. High-performance includes the pass behaviours. This station-specific grid is an AMaC teaching framework mapped to PACES skills, not an official mark scheme. Consent, hand hygiene, dignity and an appropriate chaperone are baseline professional practice. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are. A 71-year-old retired dinner lady. Practical, a little breathless, brushes things off. Lives alone since your husband died.
Opening line. "My ankles are swollen and I get out of breath. Can I just go home and see my GP?"
Volunteered. Breathless on walking for three weeks; swollen ankles; two pillows at night.

Only if asked. A heart attack seven years ago; stents. Wake at night gasping about twice a week. No chest pain now. No palpitations. No calf pain. Aspirin and atorvastatin daily; ibuprofen for your knees most days. Ex-smoker, stopped fifteen years ago. A small sherry at Christmas. No allergies. No recent travel. You do not drive today.
Hidden concern. Your husband died of heart failure and you fear the same and being a burden to your son. Reveal only if asked what worries you most.
Your questions. "Is it my heart?" "Will I need to stay in?" "Do I need a camera test?" "Can I stop the water tablet when I'm better?"
How you react. Good handling: you agree to the plan and the echo. Poor handling: if told to see your GP without a plan you say you will wait and see.

Findings (released as each step is done). Pulse 94 regular, BP 138/84, saturation 95 per cent in air, respiratory rate 20 (scenario values). JVP raised 5 cm. Bibasal crackles; dull bases. Pitting oedema to the knees. No calf swelling or tenderness. Heart sounds normal. ECG: sinus rhythm, old inferior Q waves. Chest film: cardiomegaly, upper lobe diversion, small effusions. NT-proBNP 2,400 ng/L; creatinine 98 µmol/L; potassium 4.4 mmol/L (scenario values).

Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis (R5): heart failure, probably ischaemic. Q2 Natriuretic peptide (R6): NT-proBNP above 2,000 ng/L needs specialist assessment and echocardiography within 2 weeks; 400 to 2,000 ng/L within 6 weeks (NICE NG106 diagnosis recommendations). Q3 Echo (R6): assesses valve disease and ventricular function. Q4 Treatment (R6): loop diuretic for congestion (NG106 relief of congestion recommendations); if reduced ejection fraction, offer appropriate foundational therapy with an ACE inhibitor, evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor after assessment and stabilisation with renal and electrolyte monitoring and specialist-led titration (NG106 2025 medicines recommendations). Q5 Advice (R7): influenza and pneumococcal vaccines (NG106 vaccination recommendations); do not routinely restrict sodium or fluid (NG106 lifestyle recommendations).
Curveball 1. "NT-proBNP is 900 ng/L." (R6) Safe: specialist assessment and echo within 6 weeks.
Curveball 2. "She develops severe breathlessness at rest." (R6) Safe: this is acute heart failure; admit; NICE refers to its acute heart failure guideline.
Curveball 3. "Give her ibuprofen for the knees." (R6) Safe: avoid; anti-inflammatories worsen fluid retention and kidney function.
Curveball 4. "I'm going home." (R7) Safe: she has capacity; explain risks; offer a safety net.

Fail performance
CANDIDATE: Lie down and let me look. [R1 Fail] (No history of nights or tablets. [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail])
(Reports a normal neck veins and no crackles. [R4 Fail])
CANDIDATE: It's a chest infection. [R5 Fail] See your GP. [R6 Fail]
CANDIDATE: Off you go. [R7 Fail]
Examiner note: No history, signs reported wrongly, and no diuretic or echo date for a congested woman.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine you? Sit up if that is easier. Any pain? [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Do you need pillows or wake breathless? Any chest pain? Tell me about your heart history and tablets. [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: Two pillows, and ibuprofen. My husband died of heart failure.
CANDIDATE: That's a real worry. What concerns you most? [R3 Pass]
(Checks pulse, BP, JVP, chest and legs; finds raised JVP, crackles, oedema, no calf swelling. [R4 Pass])
CANDIDATE: This looks like heart failure after your heart attack. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: I'll check a blood test for heart strain, an ECG and a chest film, give a water tablet, stop the ibuprofen, and arrange an echocardiogram within the timescale the blood test sets. [R6 Pass]

CANDIDATE: I recommend same-day senior assessment of the congestion and a monitored treatment plan. Admission or an ambulatory pathway depends on response, severity and support at home. What would you like me to explain further? [R7 Pass] (Covers her and thanks her.) [R1 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and clear. Did not name the vaccines or the two NT-proBNP timescales.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: (Cleans hands.) Hello, I'm one of the doctors. May I examine you? Sit up if that is easier. Any pain? [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Do you need pillows or wake breathless? Any chest pain? Tell me about your heart history and tablets. [R2 High]
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? Are you comfortable sitting like this? [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any palpitations, calf pain or weight change? How much ibuprofen and alcohol? [R2 High]
PATIENT: I'm afraid I'll end up like my husband.
CANDIDATE: Thank you for telling me. There is treatment that helps, and we'll plan it with you. [R3 High]
(Checks pulse, BP, JVP, chest and legs; finds raised JVP, crackles, oedema, no calf swelling. [R4 High])
(Checks heart sounds, effusion signs and liver; no fever, wheeze or calf tenderness. [R4 High])
CANDIDATE: Heart failure, but pulmonary embolism, lung disease, anaemia and kidney disease are alternatives I'll test for. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: I'll check a blood test for heart strain, an ECG and a chest film, give a water tablet, and arrange an echocardiogram within the timescale the blood test sets. [R6 High]

CANDIDATE: NT-proBNP above 2,000 ng/L needs an echo within 2 weeks; 400 to 2,000 needs it within 6 weeks. I'll give a loop diuretic, check kidney function and potassium, stop ibuprofen, and offer flu and pneumococcal vaccines. Return if breathless at rest or you gain weight quickly. [R6 High]

CANDIDATE: Options: home with this plan, admission, or waiting, which risks worsening fluid. After the echo we may add heart protective tablets. What would you like me to explain further? [R7 High] Thank you for letting me examine you. [R1 High]
Examiner note: Answered the fear of her husband's death and gave the timescales and a safety net.
R6: Discharging a congested woman with no diuretic and no echo date leaves her at risk of worsening failure.
R2: Not asking about orthopnoea and ibuprofen misses the severity and a drug cause.
R4: Reporting a normal JVP when it is raised suggests signs were assumed.
R5: A chest infection ignores the old heart attack, oedema and cardiomegaly.
R7: Instructions without options leave her without a say.
"How many pillows do you sleep on?"
"I'd give a water tablet and book the echo."
"What worries you most?"
NICE NG106 (published 12 September 2018; last updated 3 September 2025): NT-proBNP above 2,000 ng/L: specialist assessment and echocardiography within 2 weeks; 400 to 2,000 ng/L: within 6 weeks.

Diuretics for congestion (NG106 relief of congestion recommendations); ACE inhibitor, evidence-based beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor when appropriate after assessment and stabilisation for reduced ejection fraction (NG106 2025 medicines recommendations); influenza and pneumococcal vaccines (NG106 vaccination recommendations); do not routinely restrict sodium or fluid (NG106 lifestyle recommendations).

These thresholds apply to the suspected chronic HF pathway and are not waiting periods for acute decompensation. Assess the extent of congestion and need for admission today. EF is unknown until echo. If HFrEF is confirmed, the 2025 NICE regimen includes ACE inhibitor, beta-blocker, MRA and SGLT2 inhibitor as appropriate, with monitored introduction. Avoid NSAIDs and arrange early renal and electrolyte review after diuresis.
THINK: Heart failure; stable enough for the pathway?
SAY: "This looks like fluid from a weak heart; a water tablet and a blood test will help."
DO: NT-proBNP; ECG; chest film; diuretic; echo date.
NUMBERS: NT-proBNP 2,400 ng/L (scenario); above 2,000: 2 weeks; 400 to 2,000: 6 weeks (NICE NG106).
TRAP: Discharge with no plan.
FINISH: Safety net: breathless at rest, rapid weight gain.
